summary: SpaceCam is an open-source web application that makes NASA’s infrared sky accessible through interactive exploration. Users travel from a 3D Earth into SPHEREx sky maps, select an object or region, and compare observations across time and wavelengths. The application brings together SPHEREx imagery from NASA/IPAC IRSA and historical surveys including 2MASS, AllWISE, DSS2, and Pan-STARRS. Blink, swipe, animation, and difference views help users investigate apparent motion and brightness changes. Tracking tools provide exploratory light curves and motion estimates, while candidate detection highlights changes for further investigation. By connecting an immersive sky viewer with real astronomical archives, SpaceCam helps students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts explore a changing universe directly in their browser. Results are presented as exploratory candidates rather than confirmed discoveries.
details:
SpaceCam turns public astronomical archives into an interactive experience for exploring how the sky looks at different times and wavelengths. Its purpose is to make NASA SPHEREx imagery easier to explore while connecting it with historical observations of the same regions.

HOW IT WORKS

The experience begins with an interactive 3D Earth surrounded by an all-sky view. Users can navigate the sky through 72 selectable sectors, search for an object, or choose a target from a built-in catalogue of 136 objects and fields.

SpaceCam loads SPHEREx infrared maps and archive imagery from NASA/IPAC IRSA. It also provides access to 2MASS, AllWISE, DSS2, and Pan-STARRS imagery. Where archive coverage is available, users can retrieve individual SPHEREx observations and examine a region across multiple visits.

Several comparison modes make differences easier to investigate. Side-by-side views show observations together; blink and swipe modes reveal changes interactively; animations display sequences of observations; and difference views highlight residual features between aligned images. Stacking and trail views offer additional ways to inspect image sequences.

The analysis tools can follow a selected source through a sequence, plot relative brightness, and estimate apparent motion. A candidate-detection tool highlights features that may have appeared, faded, brightened, or moved. Links to the original archive resources support further investigation.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SpaceCam is designed for students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and people beginning to explore astronomical data. It brings navigation, archive access, and visual comparison into one browser interface, reducing the steps between choosing an object and investigating its observations.

The intended impact is to encourage learning through direct interaction with real data: comparing wavelengths, observing apparent stellar motion, investigating brightness changes, and understanding why repeated observations matter.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

The browser application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and WebGL. Its imaging components include HEALPix/HiPS map rendering, FITS reading, coordinate transformations, image alignment, difference imaging, and exploratory source tracking.

A Node.js proxy supports access to public NASA IRSA and JPL services. An optional Python pipeline uses scientific libraries for downloading, aligning, and processing selected example fields. The project code is available under the MIT License.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

SpaceCam combines immersive navigation with practical image-comparison tools. Users can move from a whole-sky view to a particular source and investigate its observations without switching between several separate interfaces.

The design considers archive coverage, loading time, image alignment, and differences between instruments. Observations from different surveys can vary in wavelength, resolution, sensitivity, and processing, so a visible difference does not necessarily indicate a physical change. Detection results, brightness plots, and motion estimates are exploratory and require further validation.

AI ASSISTANCE

Claude Opus and OpenAI Codex assisted with code development and revisions. OpenAI Codex also assisted with drafting the project submission text. Astronomical imagery is sourced from the credited archives.
